title: Extended Case 6 — Harnswell Quality
text:
1. The quality manager’s brief

Harnswell manufactures precision cam rollers for sewing machines.
Oversized parts may be downgraded; undersized parts may become scrap.
Source: Basic Business Statistics, ninth edition, Chapter 18, pp. 752–754.
Unit: one roller diameter, in inches; five measurements per production batch for 30 batches.
Engineering limits: 0.5072 to 0.5075 inches, inclusive.
Period: source batch order is retained; calendar dates are not supplied in the CSV.
The workbook column Day is represented here as batch, consistent with the case’s production subgroups.
Limit: the historical case narrative does not establish that temperature alone caused the observed variation.

stopifnot(nrow(rollers) == 150, all(table(rollers$batch) == 5))

USL <- .5075

title: Extended Case 6 — Harnswell Quality
text:
4. A short process-control primer

Within-batch variation concerns the five rollers in one subgroup.
Between-batch changes may indicate shifts in centering or operating conditions.
An R chart tracks within-batch ranges; an X-bar chart tracks batch means.
Check the R chart first: unstable within-batch variation undermines interpretation of X-bar limits.
Control limits estimate expected variation for a stable process; specification limits describe acceptable products.
A stable process can still produce unacceptable parts.

title: Extended Case 6 — Harnswell Quality
text:
5. Estimate initial chart limits

For subgroup size five, use A2 = 0.577, D3 = 0, D4 = 2.114.
X-bar limits: grand mean ± A2 × average range.
R limits: D3 × average range and D4 × average range.
These are initial Phase I limits estimated using all 30 batches, including any unusual batches.


subgroups <- rollers %>% group_by(batch) %>%
  summarise(xbar = mean(diameter), R = max(diameter) - min(diameter),
    n = n(), .groups = "drop") %>% arrange(batch)
stopifnot(all(subgroups$n == 5))
xbarbar <- mean(subgroups$xbar)
Rbar <- mean(subgroups$R)
xlimits <- xbarbar + c(-1, 1) * .577 * Rbar
rlimits <- c(0, 2.114 * Rbar)
knitr::kable(data.frame(chart = c("X-bar", "R"),
  centre = c(xbarbar, Rbar), lower = c(xlimits[1], rlimits[1]),
  upper = c(xlimits[2], rlimits[2])), digits = 7)

The initial X-bar chart flags batch 17 below its lower limit; the R chart has no beyond-limit point.
A signal is a reason to investigate a potential special cause.
No beyond-limit points would not by itself prove stability: runs, trends, grouping and operational context also matter.
Keep batch 17 in the original analysis; do not delete it merely to make the chart look stable.

title: Extended Case 6 — Harnswell Quality
section: 7. Capability requires a stable, suitable process model
text:
7. Capability requires a stable, suitable process model

Cp compares specification width with six within-process standard deviations.
Cpk also accounts for the process mean’s distance from each specification limit.
With subgroup size five, an estimate of within-process SD is average range / d2, where d2 = 2.326.
The initial charts signal instability, so a reliable capability claim is not supported by this initial dataset.
The following template is intentionally not executed. Use it only after a documented stability investigation and suitable distribution/measurement checks.


# stable_subgroups must come from a justified, documented process phase.
mu <- mean(stable_subgroups$xbar)
sigma_within <- mean(stable_subgroups$R) / 2.326
Cp <- (USL - LSL) / (6 * sigma_within)
Cpk <- min((USL - mu) / (3 * sigma_within),
           (mu - LSL) / (3 * sigma_within))


A negative Cpk indicates a fitted mean beyond a specification limit; it is not a negative defect percentage.
Do not convert Cp or Cpk into a guaranteed future defect rate without the additional model assumptions.

title: Extended Case 6 — Harnswell Quality
text:
8. Independent quality-improvement briefing

Reproduce specification counts and percentages from the 150 measurements.
Report the initial R and X-bar limits with units and appropriate decimal precision.
Explain how batch 17 can signal a shift even though none of its individual measurements is below specification.
Propose records to examine: temperature, warm-up, setup, tooling and measurement calibration.
The book describes a cold-start explanation and corrective action. Explain why the narrative is insufficient to prove causality in the CSV alone.
As a retrospective sensitivity analysis, recalculate limits excluding batch 17, retain the original results and state what evidence would justify treating it as a separate process condition.
Explain why recalculated limits alone do not validate future process stability or capability.
Recommend how to collect new subgroups after an intervention, and distinguish reducing variation from shifting the process mean.

title: Extended Case 6 — Harnswell Quality
text:
Submission

Specification table, both initial control charts and the flagged-batch table.
A 150–200-word improvement memo addressing stability, compliance, the source discrepancy and next measurements.
Include a justified comparison of original and sensitivity results if assigned; keep capability claims conditional.

title: Extended Case 4 — Perfect Parachute
text:
1. The procurement manager’s brief

Perfect Parachute purchases synthetic fibre from four suppliers.
Five parachutes per supplier are woven and tested to breaking point.
Source: Basic Business Statistics, ninth edition, Chapter 11, pp. 388 and 393–399.
Unit: one tested parachute; 20 measurements in four groups.
Outcome: tensile strength on the source scale; a physical force unit is not specified in the reviewed material.
Limit: small groups provide limited information about distribution shape and supplier reliability.

title: Extended Case 4 — Perfect Parachute
text:
2. Import measurement rows only

data_dir <- if (dir.exists("data")) "data" else file.path("..", "data")
source(file.path(data_dir, "..", "lessons", "_includes", "course-tools.R"))
parachutes <- read.csv(file.path(data_dir, "business", "extended-parachute.csv"))
parachutes$supplier <- factor(parachutes$supplier)
stopifnot(nrow(parachutes) == 20, all(table(parachutes$supplier) == 5))
supplier_summary <- parachutes %>% group_by(supplier) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), mean_strength = mean(strength), sd_strength = sd(strength),
    min_strength = min(strength), max_strength = max(strength), .groups = "drop")

title: Extended Case 4 — Perfect Parachute
text:
3. A short ANOVA introduction

Separate variation between supplier means from variation within suppliers.
ANOVA divides each sum of squares by its degrees of freedom to form a mean square.
F = between-group mean square / within-group mean square.
A large F is evidence against equal population means under the model.
Null: all four population mean strengths are equal.
Alternative: at least one differs; the test does not say that all pairs differ.
Classical one-way ANOVA assumes independent errors, approximately normal errors within groups and a common error variance.


fit <- aov(strength ~ supplier, data = parachutes)
summary(fit)

            Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)  
supplier     3  63.29  21.095   3.462 0.0414 *
Residuals   16  97.50   6.094                 
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1



aov() fits the one-factor model; supplier is categorical, not a numeric trend.
F is approximately 3.462, with p approximately 0.0414.
At 5%, the model gives evidence against all four means being equal.

title: Extended Case 4 — Perfect Parachute
text:
4. Which comparisons are supported?

TukeyHSD(fit)

  Tukey multiple comparisons of means
    95% family-wise confidence level

Fit: aov(formula = strength ~ supplier, data = parachutes)

$supplier
                       diff        lwr      upr     p adj
Supplier 2-Supplier 1  4.74  0.2731426 9.206857 0.0356281
Supplier 3-Supplier 1  3.32 -1.1468574 7.786857 0.1868706
Supplier 4-Supplier 1  1.64 -2.8268574 6.106857 0.7231935
Supplier 3-Supplier 2 -1.42 -5.8868574 3.046857 0.8000982
Supplier 4-Supplier 2 -3.10 -7.5668574 1.366857 0.2340709
Supplier 4-Supplier 3 -1.68 -6.1468574 2.786857 0.7084910



Tukey’s procedure adjusts pairwise intervals and tests for the family of comparisons under the ANOVA assumptions.
Read each contrast’s direction and interval; do not rank suppliers using p-values alone.
An overall significant test need not make every pair significant.
These intervals concern mean differences, not minimum guaranteed product strength.

title: Extended Case 4 — Perfect Parachute
section: 5. Check the model and its limits
text:
5. Check the model and its limits

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(fit, which = 1)
plot(fit, which = 2)







par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
fligner.test(strength ~ supplier, data = parachutes)


    Fligner-Killeen test of homogeneity of variances

data:  strength by supplier
Fligner-Killeen:med chi-squared = 0.55853, df = 3, p-value = 0.9059



Residual plots assess spread and approximate normality; they cannot establish independent assignment.
fligner.test() checks dispersion; a large p-value does not prove equal variances.
Five observations per supplier give imprecise diagnostics.
Causal supplier claims need a defensible assignment protocol and control of weaving/testing conditions.


Optional: relax the equal-variance assumption

oneway.test(strength ~ supplier, data = parachutes, var.equal = FALSE)


    One-way analysis of means (not assuming equal variances)

data:  strength and supplier
F = 3.3206, num df = 3.0000, denom df = 8.7743, p-value = 0.07206



Welch’s one-way test avoids assuming equal variances.
Tukey intervals from the classical model do not automatically become Welch-compatible pairwise intervals.
Report sensitivity openly rather than choosing the method giving the preferred answer.

title: Extended Case 4 — Perfect Parachute
text:
6. Independent procurement briefing

Explain F using the observed between- and within-supplier variation.
Identify the largest sample mean difference and report its Tukey interval and adjusted p-value.
Compare classical and Welch conclusions, including their assumptions.
Explain why five tests per supplier cannot establish rare failure rates or minimum guaranteed strength.
Specify additional evidence on cost, delivery reliability and engineering requirements before recommending a supplier.
Propose a follow-up experiment controlling loom conditions and assigning fibre treatments appropriately.

title: Extended Case 4 — Perfect Parachute
section: 7. Optional design discussion: supplier and loom
text:
7. Optional design discussion: supplier and loom

The book also considers four suppliers and two loom types.
The local Parachute2 workbook contains a separate Data sheet with loom-level observations as well as summary sheets.
This case analyses the original one-way, 20-measurement dataset; it does not combine the two experiments.
A supplier-by-loom interaction means the supplier difference depends on loom type.
Discuss how an interaction would change procurement advice; a two-factor analysis is beyond this assignment.

title: Extended Case 4 — Perfect Parachute
text:
Submission

Supplier summary table, one chart and a brief explanation of the overall and pairwise results.
A 150-word procurement memo with a practical threshold, assumptions and a proposed follow-up.
If a minimum strength threshold is not supplied, request one; do not invent an engineering requirement.

title: Extended Case 2 — Oxford Cereal
text:
1. The packaging manager’s brief

Oxford fills cereal boxes labelled 368 grams.
Underfilling concerns customers; overfilling uses extra product.
Source: Basic Business Statistics, ninth edition, Chapters 7 (p. 232) and 9 (pp. 296–303; numerical example p. 302).
Reported evidence: 25 boxes, sample mean 372.5 g, assumed known population SD 15 g.
Unit: grams per box; the supplied CSV has one summary row, not 25 box records.
Limit: raw weights, collection dates and individual underfill counts are unavailable.
The publisher’s separate CEREALS cost/nutrition dataset is not Oxford packaging data.

stopifnot(n == 25, sigma == 15, mu0 == 368, xbar == 372.5)


Summary CSV · Data guide.
sigma is assumed known in the textbook example; it is not estimated from these 25 boxes.
A Z procedure requires the stated known SD and an appropriate sampling/normal model.

title: Extended Case 2 — Oxford Cereal
section: 3. Separate variation between boxes and between sample means

3. Separate variation between boxes and between sample means

se <- sigma / sqrt(n)
knitr::kable(data.frame(sample_size = n, sample_mean_g = xbar,
  difference_from_target_g = xbar - mu0, process_sd_g = sigma,
  standard_error_g = se), digits = 2)

process_sd_g

sigma = 15 g describes variation between individual boxes under the model.
se = 3 g describes variation between means of independent samples of 25 boxes.
Increasing sample size reduces the standard error; it does not mechanically reduce process variation.

title: Extended Case 2 — Oxford Cereal
text:
4. See the sampling distribution

This simulation generates hypothetical normal-process weights under a 368 g mean and 15 g SD.
Its values are not observed Oxford measurements.


set.seed(42001)
sim_means <- replicate(10000, mean(rnorm(n, mean = mu0, sd = sigma)))
ggplot(data.frame(sample_mean = sim_means), aes(sample_mean)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 35, fill = petra_accent, colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = xbar, colour = petra_ink, linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Mean of 25 simulated boxes (g)", y = "Simulated samples")









set.seed() makes the simulation reproducible.
replicate() repeats the hypothetical sampling experiment.
The vertical line marks the reported sample mean, 372.5 g.

title: Extended Case 2 — Oxford Cereal
text:
5. Test the process mean

Null: the population mean is 368 g.
Alternative: the population mean differs from 368 g.
Decision threshold: 5%, two-sided.


z <- (xbar - mu0) / se
p_value <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(z))
ci <- xbar + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(1 - alpha / 2) * se
knitr::kable(data.frame(z = z, p_value = p_value,
  lower_mean_g = ci[1], upper_mean_g = ci[2], reject = p_value < alpha), digits = 4)




z
p_value
lower_mean_g
upper_mean_g
reject




1.5
0.1336
366.6201
378.3799
FALSE






pnorm() gives the normal tail probability; the two tails account for deviations in either direction.
The result is Z = 1.50, with p about 0.134.
The 95% interval for the process mean is approximately 366.62–378.38 g.
The evidence is insufficient to reject the 368 g mean at 5% under the stated assumptions.
This does not prove exact centering, individual-box compliance or a low underfill rate.

title: Extended Case 2 — Oxford Cereal
text:
6. Independent packaging review

Explain why sd() or t.test() on the single summary row cannot analyse 25 individual boxes.
Recalculate the test and interval for a hypothetical sample mean of 375 g, holding the other inputs fixed.
Compare the standard errors for hypothetical independent sample sizes 25 and 100 with the same known process SD.
Explain why a narrow interval for the mean does not guarantee that individual boxes meet a weight requirement.
Describe Type I and Type II errors as unnecessary process intervention and missed process changes.
Specify the raw measurements and sampling records needed to investigate underfilling and process stability.

title: Part 1: Introduction to R
text:
1.2 Objects, vectors and missing values

Save and calculate

<- saves a value; R distinguishes uppercase from lowercase.
Quoted text is character data. TRUE and FALSE are logical values.
The following values are illustrative planning inputs, not extra Superstore records.


unit_price <- 25
units <- 4
sales_value <- unit_price * units
sales_value

[1] 100

business_question <- "Which categories generate profit?"
sales_value > 80

[1] TRUE




Work with several values

# Illustrative order values, in dollars.
order_values <- c(25, 60, 100, 250)
mean(order_values)

[1] 108.75

median(order_values)

[1] 80

order_values[1]                    # R starts counting at 1

[1] 25

order_values[order_values >= 100]   # Keep entries meeting a condition

[1] 100 250



==: equals; !=: differs; &: AND; |: OR; %in%: belongs to a set.
NA means missing. It is different from zero.
Check why a value is missing before excluding it.


values_with_missing <- c(25, 60, NA, 250)
is.na(values_with_missing)

[1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE

mean(values_with_missing)                 # Missingness propagates

[1] NA

mean(values_with_missing, na.rm = TRUE)   # Mean of the observed values only

[1] 111.6667

sum(is.na(values_with_missing))

[1] 1

title: Part 1: Introduction to R
text:
1.3 Import the retail data

Download the order-line CSV.
One row is one product line within an order.
One order can have several lines. One customer can place several orders.
Use the supplied CSV so your results match the course’s pinned version.


# This cell works from the project root or the lessons/ folder.
data_dir <- if (dir.exists("data")) "data" else file.path("..", "data")
source(file.path(data_dir, "..", "lessons", "_includes", "course-tools.R"))
lines <- read.csv(file.path(data_dir, "business", "superstore-lines.csv"),
                  stringsAsFactors = FALSE, colClasses = c(postal_code = "character"))
orders <- make_orders(lines)
c(order_lines = nrow(lines), orders = nrow(orders),
  customers = n_distinct(lines$customer_id))

read.csv() creates a data frame: variables in columns, records in rows.
source() loads the shared chart style and the explained order-summary function.
make_orders() checks agreement of order attributes and sums sales, profit and units within each order.
It calculates shipping time from order date to ship date; this is not delivery time.

title: Part 1: Introduction to R

1.4 Select, filter and create variables

select() chooses columns.
filter() chooses rows.
mutate() adds or transforms variables.
%>% passes the result of one step to the next.


loss_lines <- lines %>%
  filter(profit < 0) %>%

title: Extended Case 3 — BLK Retail Display

1. The merchandising manager’s brief

BLK cola is sold in normal-shelf and end-of-aisle displays.
Source: Basic Business Statistics, ninth edition, Chapter 10, pp. 336–339.
Design: 20 selected stores of similar sales volume; random assignment of ten stores to each condition.
Unit: one store observed for one week; outcome is cases sold per week.
Limit: random selection from all supermarkets is not established, and one week does not establish long-term effects.
Business question: Does the sales gain warrant further consideration of the display space?

The estimated difference is end aisle minus normal: 21.7 cases per store per week.
The Welch 95% interval is about 6.57–36.83 cases, with p about 0.00785.
The two-sided null is equal mean sales under the two conditions.
The book uses a pooled-variance t test; the course uses Welch, which avoids the equal-variance assumption.
Random assignment supports the experimental contrast among these stores, subject to implementation and no interference.
Sales evidence alone does not establish the display’s net commercial value.

Each group contains only ten stores; Q-Q plots have limited power to reveal departures from normality.
Independence follows from the design and store operations, not from a normality plot.
Check whether stores could affect one another’s sales or whether promotions differed.
Do not choose a paired test because the original spreadsheet aligned two columns.

title: Extended Case 3 — BLK Retail Display
text:
5. Independent commercial briefing

Reproduce the effect, confidence interval and p-value, with units and direction.
Run the textbook’s pooled test using var.equal = TRUE; compare its interval and assumptions with Welch’s.
Run a Wilcoxon rank-sum comparison. Explain why it is not generally a test of equality of means.
Define the population to which you can reasonably discuss the results; distinguish assignment from selection.
Complete the commercial sensitivity analysis below and recommend a next step.


Hypothetical commercial assumptions

Contribution margin per additional case: $4, $6 or $8.
Opportunity cost of the display: $80 per store per week.
These are assignment assumptions, not COLA observations or textbook financial data.
Assume the measured sales difference represents incremental cases and the chosen margin applies to them; discuss why this may fail.


margin_per_case <- c(4, 6, 8)
display_cost <- 80
# For each assumed margin, calculate:
# estimated net contribution = estimated case difference * margin - cost
# corresponding interval endpoints = Welch endpoints * margin - cost
# break-even additional cases = cost / margin


Multiplying the sales interval by a fixed positive margin gives a conditional interval under that assumed margin.
It does not include uncertainty in costs, margins, cannibalization or future display effects.
Treat a zero-crossing interval as uncertainty about the assumed commercial threshold, not proof of no value.

Inspect curvature, changing residual spread, unusual residuals and influential rows.
Row numbers identify records; they are not verified timestamps.
A diagnostic flag is a reason to investigate, not an automatic rule for deleting a measurement.


A direct collinearity check

predictor_names <- names(potato)[names(potato) != "solids"]
vif <- sapply(predictor_names, function(variable) {
  others <- setdiff(predictor_names, variable)
  1 / (1 - summary(lm(reformulate(others, variable), data = potato))$r.squared)
})

Each VIF compares a predictor with the other predictors; it measures variance inflation from their linear overlap.
Large VIFs warn that holding the other predictors fixed may describe combinations with little support in the data.
VIF does not assess omitted confounding or establish a causal model.

title: Extended Case 5 — Mountain States Potato
text:
8. Independent production briefing

Report the mean solids and the percentages below, and at or below, 12%; explain the denominator.
Identify the strongest predictor overlaps using correlations and VIFs.
Interpret one coefficient from the full model in correct units, including what is held constant.
Compare full and reduced models using fit, diagnostics and process interpretability.
Investigate the most influential record. If you fit a sensitivity model without it, retain and report the original full-data model too.
Propose additional data collection with timestamps, day IDs and relevant operating conditions.
Design a controlled follow-up investigation of one promising factor within feasible operating ranges.

Submission

One model-comparison table and two charts serving different questions.
A 150–200-word executive summary distinguishing observed association, uncertain prediction and proposed controlled investigation.
Do not recommend immediately changing plant settings based solely on these observational regressions.
